content: Your doctor has prescribed cefuroxime, an antibiotic, to treat your infection. This medication will either be injected into a large muscle, such as your buttock or hip, or administered intravenously through a needle or catheter placed in your vein. The intravenous infusion will typically last for 30 minutes and may be given two to four times a day. Cefuroxime works by eliminating bacteria responsible for various infections, including those affecting the lungs, skin, bones, joints, stomach, blood, and urinary tract. In some cases, this medication may be prescribed for other uses; consult your doctor or pharmacist for additional information. Your healthcare provider may monitor the effectiveness of your treatment and check for side effects through laboratory tests and physical examinations. It is crucial to attend all scheduled appointments with your doctor and the laboratory. The duration of your treatment will depend on how your infection and symptoms respond to the medication. Before starting cefuroxime, inform your doctor and pharmacist if you are allergic to cefuroxime, other cephalosporins, penicillins, or any other drugs. Additionally, provide a list of all prescription and nonprescription medications you are taking, especially other antibiotics, probenecid (Benemid), and vitamins. Notify your doctor if you have a history of kidney, liver, or gastrointestinal diseases, particularly colitis. If you are pregnant, planning to become pregnant, or breastfeeding, inform your doctor. If you become pregnant while taking cefuroxime, contact your doctor immediately. If you have diabetes and regularly check your urine for sugar, use Clinistix or TesTape, as cefuroxime may cause false-positive results with Clinitest tablets. Before administering cefuroxime, inspect the solution carefully. It should be clear and free of any floating particles. Gently squeeze the bag or check the container to ensure there are no leaks. Do not use the solution if it is discolored, contains particles, or if the bag or container is leaking. Use a new solution and show the damaged one to your healthcare provider. It is essential to follow your medication instructions precisely. Do not stop your treatment without consulting your healthcare provider, as this could worsen your infection and potentially lead to hospitalization. Do not alter your dosing schedule without discussing it with your healthcare provider. If you experience a mechanical problem, such as a blockage in the tubing, needle, or catheter, your healthcare provider may instruct you to stop the infusion. If this occurs, contact your healthcare provider immediately to ensure your therapy continues. Cefuroxime may cause side effects. If you are receiving the medication via intramuscular injection, it may be mixed with lidocaine (Xylocaine) to reduce pain at the injection site. Notify your healthcare provider if you experience any of the following minor side effects, especially if they are severe or persistent: diarrhea, stomach pain, upset stomach, or vomiting. If you experience any of the following severe side effects, contact your healthcare provider immediately: unusual bleeding or bruising, difficulty breathing, itching, rash, hives, or a sore mouth or throat. Serious side effects can be reported to the FDA’s MedWatch Adverse Event Reporting program online or by phone. If you are receiving cefuroxime intravenously, you will likely be instructed to store it in the refrigerator or freezer. Take your next dose out of the refrigerator one hour before use and place it in a clean, dry area to allow it to reach room temperature. If additional cefuroxime is stored in the freezer, move a 24-hour supply to the refrigerator for the next day’s use. Do not refreeze medications. If you are receiving cefuroxime intramuscularly, your healthcare provider will provide specific storage instructions. Store your medication only as directed and ensure you understand the proper storage requirements. Keep your supplies in a clean, dry place when not in use, and keep all medications and supplies out of reach of children. Your healthcare provider will instruct you on how to safely dispose of used needles, syringes, tubing, and containers to prevent accidental injury. In case of an overdose, contact your local poison control center at 1-800-222-1222. If the individual has collapsed or is not breathing, call emergency services at 911. If you are receiving cefuroxime intravenously or subcutaneously, it is important to recognize the symptoms of a catheter-related infection, which occurs at the site where the needle enters your vein or skin.
